pitch_detail.notes: Follow the crack up toward the chimney and set the belay at the chimney's base. Gear used was a #2, a #3 and a nut. It may be possible to run this together with the next pitch.

Stem and climb the box chimney, then break out left near its top and work up a short face section to a small stance. Loose blocks sit here (the only ones on the route) and should be pulled off. Belay above them in a solid crack; a single #3 plus other pieces is enough, since the second #3 ends up in the anchor.

Climb the clean, sharply cut corner to a rest, where you can also belay out to the right. Continue straight up the splitter crack; it narrows and steepens, and face holds then lead to the top. The belay is set well back on the ledge.

review.changed: Wrote all 3 pitches with grades and gear hints; no lengths or bolt counts stated, none written.
review.other_findings: None; descent (walk off right) matches stored.

pitch_detail.notes: Pick any of the many hand cracks in the corner system and follow them to a small perch about halfway up the system.
Keep going up the right-hand face, which is covered in hand cracks of various lines; you drift right as you climb but almost any path works. The belay is closer to hanging, taken wherever is easiest.
The cracks steepen slightly and give sustained jamming with good position. Staying on the far-right cracks leads to an exit around the arete onto a roomy ledge.
Climb the corner leaving the ledge (a bit grainy), then angle up and left as the slope eases, taking the easiest line toward the top.
Continue up and left toward the summit. A small corner takes you nearly to the top, then a few jugs lead onto the summit block.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches with grades and lengths (m as stated).

pitch_detail.notes: Go up and left along the red streak, passing a pocket that accepts a cam, then thin gear to a wide ledge. Belay at the ledge's far right end, above a small sapling. Runout.
Trend right over a small overlap, then back left to a broken stance beneath the wide roof/flake. Protection is reasonable (PG). Large pieces help build the belay here.
Climb the beautiful red slab, using a cam pocket and a single quarter-inch bolt. A short runout gives way to easier cracks; belay at Two Tree ledge by stepping right.

Climb easy corners, then a diagonal hand/fist crack heading left across polished gold rock, then up to a big ledge. After this, 4th class scrambling for about 300 ft reaches the summit of Falls Ridge East.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches. Rappels not listed station by station (none written).
review.other_findings: descent_text is null on the row; the text gives a descent: from the summit follow the northeast ridge to an easy gully traversing back along the base (about 40 min), or a forested gully to climber's left below the summit headwall.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin in the flake angling left and enter the A-frame feature's right side, which a roof caps. Gear is sporty. Get over the roof and belay next to bolts of doubtful quality.

Step left to an odd groove-crack and follow it to a sloping ledge (optional belay). Then a steep stemming/finger-crack box leads to a good bolt and a big roof. The roof is hard; easier climbing past it reaches a good two-bolt anchor.
This is the corner visible from the base. Some bouldery steps begin it, then a sustained groove follows. Belay from a stance on a dike.

Keep following the corner as the difficulty builds. Escape the roof via its right edge into a layback, climb that until a step right into a neighbouring crack system makes sense, then take it to a hanging stance with two good bolts. Some rate this pitch as hard as 5.11b.
Angle left into the evident corner packed with flakes, ribs and grooves. Past the intimidating flake near its top, move right to a little ledge for the belay.

Look for the prow beneath the Finger; a narrow V-groove on its left widens to hand size. Traverse up and left to reach it and climb to the good ledge above for the belay. The moves are technical and involve some shimmying.

Move right and take the crack running up the Finger's right flank. The lower moves are spicy for 5.8. Wide-looking higher up, it still takes a solid #3 once you are standing in it. Stop anywhere on the North Ridge to belay.

review.changed: Wrote 7 pitches. Listed grades are the topo's; the climbers who wrote it felt most pitches ran about a grade harder (lichen, flared cracks). Omitted the scrambling to the summit block (a couple of short finishes, 5.8 or 5.7).
review.other_findings: descent_text null on the row; text gives none.

pitch_detail.notes: Short pitch: a hand crack on the big chimney's left side ends at a sandy ledge that slopes and holds loose rocks.
Loose, sandy scrambling on blocky ground for roughly 100 ft until the rock cleans up at the chimney's top. Rope up or not as you judge.
Head left up easy ledges to a nice layback onto a narrow ledge; a clean chimney sits at its west end.
Squeeze up the chimney, then follow the narrow ridge behind with great exposure, finishing with a flake move to the tiny summit.

rappel_detail.station: about 10 ft below the summit on the southeast side
rappel_detail.notes: Brings you down to the loose, sandy class 3 section. Sharp rock here has nearly cut a rope, so weigh rappelling against downclimbing.

rappel_detail.station: set into the large chimney's east wall
rappel_detail.notes: A short rappel that gets you below the pitch 1 hand crack. Mind rope-cutting edges.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches and a 2-station rappel list.
review.other_findings: descent_text null on the row; the text gives two rappels (above).

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the crack/corner straight up to a belay on a big block or ramp that leads toward the next pitch. An approach pitch of about 45 m comes first.
A slabby ramp leads to a corner; go up and left along it and belay right beneath the crux pitch.
The crux. Steep corner cracks with good gear, belaying at a stance (a .3 to #1 Camelot works there).
Follow the arete and crack systems to the top, then easy snow ramp to a belay on a slung block or tree.
Easy ridge scrambling: go up and left from the belay around the rock called the bunny ears, then up and right with an unprotected traverse to a so-so belay spot before the next pitch.
Tougher snow, then fun ridge romping to a pyramid-shaped rock that makes a great sling anchor.
Ridge climbing; extend all your pieces because rope drag is the main difficulty.
Easy ridge romp to the summit with good protection, though loose rock becomes more common higher.

review.changed: Wrote 8 pitches; the ~45 m approach pitch is mentioned in P1. Grades listed for pitches 1-5 follow each description's trailing line; P6-8 ungraded. Lengths are approximate (~).
review.other_findings: Row grade M6 but the crux pitch is stated as M7. Pitches 6-8 are optional to rope (competent parties may move together).

pitch_detail.notes: Steep opening on good holds, then several awkward mantles and a brief finger crack to end. Traverse up and right to reach the anchor, which is bolted.
Long slab straight up from the anchor, a tricky roof pull, then on to the top of the wall and a two-bolt anchor. 21 bolts on the pitch.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches. Descent: three rappels down the neighbouring route to the left, but no stations listed, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: A wide crack gains a ledge; clip a bolt, then stem and jam a corner that becomes a splitter flake-crack. Once it runs out, bolts protect the roof, and a slab finishes at a belay that hangs slightly. Worth doing as a one-pitch outing.

Low-angle broken rock with good placements leads to a dihedral that faces and leans right. Bolts cover most of the dihedral, which you climb with a mix of jamming and face moves on its right wall. A bulge near the top, then technical dikes reach an anchor at a big flake.
This is the first pitch of the Emperor.
Follow the obvious dike out to the right.

Powerful moves leave the belay up and left into a corner that takes you to the large flake overhead; rope drag is a concern. Then traverse right onto the face above, and at the bush go right once more to finish in the groove.
The easiest pitch: a right-facing corner to the belay.
Hard moves off the belay past a few bolts, then into a dike with more bolts. Leave the dike aiming for the roof and finish at a stance.

Climb the corner and make delicate moves out left at the top, then two more bolts above. Higher, the climbing splits. The right variation climbs the dihedral directly, needing odd footwork or knee bars (about 5.12+, and the one used for the first free ascent); the left is a touch harder and calls for a horizontal mantle.
Climb through the roof, then directly right toward the obvious bulge mid-face. Step down to better footholds off poor hands, then continue right on easy ground until you meet What's Up Bubb.
The crux pitch of What's Up Bubb.
Leave the belay leftward through a roof of grainy rock, then trace the clear tufa line to the next belay.
Round the corner to the right into stepped dihedrals, clipping bolts for roughly 50 ft, then knobs and broken terrain reach the belay.
Easy climbing to link back with What's Up Bubb and, further up, the upper two pitches of the Emperor to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote the 11 pitches the text describes (no lengths stated). No rappel table: descent is described only as rappelling to the bottom of pitch 9 then following What's Up Bubb's rappels, with a 70 m rope and tag line.
review.other_findings: Stored pitches 14, text lists 11 (P11 folds in the Emperor's upper two). Stored descent says the lower stations are all bolted; the text says rappel from the top to the base of pitch 9.

pitch_detail.notes: Shared with Ikigai. Crux right from the deck up to a chockstone's top; easy scrambling gets you behind the chimney to a bolt, then you stem past three further bolts, finishing at an anchor with two bolts. About 100 ft (rough guess).

Scramble the gully for about 20 ft, then a short face and an awkward mantle gain a ramp. The ramp heads up and right past one more bolt to a left-facing dihedral, where the widening hand crack goes at 5.10. Then descend slightly and traverse left to an anchor of two bolts on a fine ledge. About 70 ft.

The Seam. Easy ground past a couple of bolts (5.10a to 5.11a depending on height), then 5.9 cracks on medium cams to a ledge. Tiptoe up the technical seam past five more bolts to a sloping belay. About 80 ft.

Ikigai's Dave Slab pitches are an alternative; this route splits from them here. Take the right-trending, right-facing dihedral straight up to a #5 BD layback (5.7 R), or slip out right onto a thin flake (5.9) to a ledge anchored by two bolts. About 90 ft.
The dihedral continues into a juggy golden chimney that turns into a face; then traverse hard right on a ledge to rejoin Ikigai above its mantle. Easy, but a fall would swing the second. About 90 ft.
Ikigai's crux pitch. Hand-size gear, then steep bolted face to a belay ledge with two bolts. About 80 ft.

Zig Zag Pitch. Start at the belay's right with an easy right-facing dihedral, then go left over a golden bulge (crux) with two bolts. Cut hard left and down along dikes to a bolt, mount the ramp, clip a second bolt and downclimb about 10 ft so you can move left into a left-facing dihedral (awkward, 5.10+). Fingers and hand crack lead up the pillar to a two-bolt belay near a trapped block. About 90 ft.
Pass under the roof and leave it leftward into powerful, exposed laybacking with bolts, reaching a right-leaning ramp and a good ledge beside a left-facing corner. About 100 ft.

Continue up Ikigai (steep 5.9), then go well right and up to a lone bolt, an easy (5.5) downclimb ramp and a 5.9 step right onto Inseguimento Ledge. About 100 ft. Optional rappel of roughly 190 ft from the ledge, descending toward climber's left to a two-bolt anchor at the far left end of a long ledge.

Layback to the crack (5.11a), jam fingers then hands until you can step right onto a dike ledge. Go up and right into a corner that is the crux, onto a ledge, then more hard climbing (5.11a). At the big hollow flake either climb straight past a bolt to link with the next pitch, or skip the bolt and belay left above a bush. About 100 ft.

Hollow flake first, then a thin finger crack up to a bolt (5.11a) and a left-facing dihedral protected by medium gear. When the dihedral bends right, go straight up and left on bolts into the Golden Shield Headwall, which holds the crux, ending on a sloping ledge where two bolts form the anchor. About 80 ft.

Go straight up past a bolt onto thin, technical gear climbing, to a belay with two bolts just before the crack veers hard right. Can be combined with the next pitch, but you will want your full gear. About 70 ft.

Easy climbing along a right-trending low-angle dihedral past a couple of bushes, then fingers as the crack turns vertical, then tips (crux) and maybe a medium piece, to a two-bolt anchor at a stance. About 110 ft.

Walking on Sunshine. Climb the left-hand crack (bolts), then traverse hard right to a thin crack (crux, bolts) ending on a ledge beneath a big roof. Medium, then tips/finger cams to the roof; layback out it into more laybacking on golden granite with a couple of bolts, thin to medium gear and more bolts. After a flake, an anchor of two bolts sits at a good stance. About 130 ft.
The Trio: two golden dikes. Climb them, escaping left to an anchor with two bolts on a good ledge capping the headwall. About 90 ft. Lower-angle ground continues to the top.

Go straight up on bolts, just to the right of a crack that bottoms out. When that crack veers right past a bad bolt, head up and left past another bolt (5.9) and a short crack to a good belay on a prominent pillar on the skyline. About 90 ft.

Angle up and left to a first bolt set high, which puts you on a lengthy dike, and follow the dike until you can step right (bolt) onto an easy hand crack that bends left. Climb the face straight up (bolt) to an anchor of two bolts on a good ledge. About 130 ft.
Take either of two cracks up to a bolt, then step left into a left-facing corner of finger and hand cracks, ending at a nice ledge with a two-bolt anchor. About 60 ft.
Keep going straight up, bending left to meet Ikigai on a big ledge; easy ground then reaches Ikigai's summit tree. About 180 ft.

review.changed: Wrote all 19 pitches. Lengths left in the notes (as approximate feet) because the text says they are rough guesses. No rappel table: only a partial rappel option from Inseguimento Ledge is given.
review.other_findings: None. Pitches 1-3 are shared with Ikigai.

pitch_detail.notes: Ice about 55 m long.
About 60 m, mostly WI2 with one WI3 step.
About 60 m, WI2 and perhaps slightly harder in places.
Easier, WI2- with mixed snow. From here you can continue or exit climber's left via 3rd class ledges to get off the peak.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches; lengths per the text; pitch length and difficulty depend on how thick the ice is. No rappel table (V-threads mentioned only in general).
review.other_findings: None. Row grade WI3 M1-2; text only mentions a WI3 step.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin on a detached little tower. A brief hand traverse on a crack spans a steep gully to reach a large ledge; then walk left and belay on gear.
Hand crack in the left wall; dirty in places but good. Belay behind a giant chockstone.
Three-dimensional stemming from the belay. Links with the next pitch using a 70 m rope.
Delicate climbing on small gear to a nice crack system. Leave Cinco de Mayo and move out right to a bolted anchor at a stance.
The clear flake studded with chicken heads goes up and right. Expect 5 bolts, supplemented by gear and one slung chicken head, then a belay on bolts.

An easy flake reaches a small ledge, then a hollow flake with a nice crack. A roof follows with a finger crack that becomes crimps and side pulls, on toward the next roof; flakes then lead left and up to a big dike where the belay is bolted. 8 bolts plus gear; extend pieces with care. The crux moves can be pulled through.
Traverse right along the dike past 5 bolts and one #0.5 placement near the end. Bolted belay before the junction with the West Face route.
Step right with a face move onto the West Face crack. A hand crack on the flake's right side takes you to a great ledge, belaying from pitons.
A short but burly crack leads to a great hand crack and a ledge in an alcove under an overhang. Gear belay. The grade is given as 5.8 to 5.10.
Awesome moves past the roof to a splitter to the summit. The bolted rap anchor on the far side of loose blocks can serve as a belay.

review.changed: Wrote 10 pitches with lengths from feet. Pitches 8-10 may be linked in any combination; the best ledge is atop P8. Pitch 3 and 4 can be linked with a 70 m rope.

pitch_detail.notes: Flakes lead to a pinnacle's top, where a bolt protects face moves into a crack with an undercling. Follow it right, laybacking flaky rock, to an anchor on a slab beneath the obvious P2 crack. About 200 ft; the grade is an estimate.
Take the crack, then work around the arete to the left. A bolt protects thin cracks that gradually angle up and right to a belay ledge. Length unknown; grade an estimate.
Series of cracks: stay right, then move left via a nice finger crack to a ledge with splitters above; climb them and continue up. A long pitch, possibly about 200 ft; grade uncertain (about 5.9).
Go left off the belay toward the obvious corner above; belay where the angle eases. Maybe 120 ft; grade an estimate.
Many options; one line takes the corner, then veers left to the top. A short pitch, perhaps 50 ft.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches; grades and lengths are the original authors' estimates; P3 grade left off and lengths only where stated firmly.

pitch_detail.notes: Start a few feet left of the 4th class gully of the neighbouring route; head up low-angle face into an open dihedral, over a small roof, to a bolted belay.
Head hard left along a dike, gain a crack trending back up right, and at its top move left on xenolith inclusions to a scooped ledge with a bolted anchor.

Cracks in the face and in a right-facing dihedral lead to a roof, passed by a wide stem. More cracks and features reach a huge feldspar dike; a bolt sits below it and an intermediate anchor above. Finish by traversing the dike leftward for 30-40 ft to a second bolted anchor.
Follow the wide crack from the anchor (no wide gear or climbing needed) to another bolted anchor.

Keep following the crack beyond an old leaper piton. Cracks break up but the going is easy, so hop between systems as needed. Set a gear anchor on a small, pleasant stance right under a big bulge; the next pitch's first bolt is 15-20 ft above that bulge.

Reach the bolt over the steep bulge on holds better than they look. Then traverse left with long runouts across multiple crack systems, building a gear anchor wherever one fits. Runout, with tricky route-finding.
Keep moving left across more crack systems, find the single bolt, and continue up to a bolted anchor under a steep headwall. Questing and runout.
Climb past fat bolts to a dark hand-size crack cutting the overhanging headwall, bolt-protected. An optional anchor sits just above the overhanging crack section.
Follow bolts up and right over steep but featured terrain, then more bolts up a stemming groove to a bolted anchor.

Crack and groove; gear is thin at the beginning but improves once you hit flakes. A second stemming groove, partly bolted, leads to an alcove with a triangular roof. Good jams get you through it, then an easy crack trends left before you cut back right on easier-angled face to an anchor of bolts sitting on a rounded arete.

Ramp rightward to the foot of a steep groove with bolts; stem it to a bolted anchor on a sloping ledge. A better belay is about 30 ft higher, past that anchor, where you can build a gear anchor in the blocks on the bivy ledge. Scramble to the summit afterward.

review.changed: Wrote 11 labelled pitches (the text splits pitch 8 into 8a and 8b, both ending at an anchor) with lengths from feet.
review.other_findings: Stored pitch count 10, text describes 11 (8a and 8b). Long runouts on moderate pitches.

pitch_detail.notes: Start at the right-hand end of the low, long roof on the face's west side, follow broken cracks, crossing The Knobivore, and slabs to the left edge of a gray-black slab flanked by shallow corners. Take the left corner to the roof, then the weakness above to a spacious ledge by a left-facing corner; the gear at this belay is tricky.

Work up the corner, step right around a roof, climb slabs and turn another roof on the right, then follow the weakness to the large roof. Two crack options cross it: skip the fat-finger crack and instead move left again to the hand crack. Belay on an acceptable stance after clearing the roof.
Left, then up a right-hand crack, trending right to a small roof. Pull over it and head up and right to a secure belay among huge flakes. Beyond, the angle relaxes into mostly 2nd and 3rd class.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches, no grades or lengths stated. The easy terrain above (the text calls it P4, P5) is left out; it is a romp north with a few downclimbing moves to a sandy area, then an exit by slabs and a gully.

pitch_detail.notes: Short face climb to a vertical crack system just left of a more broken one. Belay on an ample ledge system.

Traverse left on slabs, then up and left to reach the gully/corner system above the stacked-block mess, and finish up the corner. Skip the arch-like left-facing corner on the right: reaching it means leaning on a detached, person-size block.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches; only P1 length stated.

pitch_detail.notes: Start just right of the 200+ ft left-facing corner, scrambling to a smaller corner/crack system and over its small roof. Work up and left to another crack system, then left again when it ends, finishing in the crack just right of the big corner's edge, with see-through spots. Belay in small huecoed stances under a little roof.
Continue up the crack on the left through the roof to double cracks (the crux) and a belay ledge on the left.
Overhanging short crack right above the belay, then right and into the leaning slot cutting the roof band to the left. Belay on decent stances either side of the flat chockstone in the wide crack.
Escape route via the left gully: from above the chockstone, move hard left into the gray gully and climb to a belay in a sandy corridor. Easy, crumbly, about 100 ft.

Direct option: from vertical parallel hand/finger cracks under stacked noses, climb up, step left at the first nose and up its left side, then right into a short overhanging corner crack (a #4 helps at the exit). About 50 ft more on easier ground leads to a spacious belay at a notch/groove. About 80 ft.

review.changed: Wrote P1-P3 and the two alternate fourth pitches (4a, 4b).

pitch_detail.notes: Climb to the left-hand flake and step left, then discontinuous cracks and orange face lead to a stance at the foot of a flake/crack system arching left. Variation: take the right-facing corner system; where gear ends, step onto orange rock, then left via cracks and flakes to the same belay (about 5.7, solid protection).

Take the arching crack and step left where cracks cut across the overlap, then up and left to two cracks, a hand crack and a #4 crack going up right. Choose the hand crack that widens and curves left (not the flowery corner). Reach the roof, make a short awkward traverse and settle on a stance to the right.

Angle up the right-hand crack; tough moves link crack systems, heading up and right, to a belay under a roof made by a block jammed in the corner. Fixed nuts are here. A variation heads left toward Gas Chromatographer: stem the inset alcove, step left to a ledge beneath steep cracks and flakes, and finish on ample ledges (about 5.9, 60 ft).
Up giant blocks and a short stout crack system until you can trend left on easier ground to the centre of the tower. Belay on ample ledges.
Scamper to the top of the tower, then 3rd class scrambling toward the northwest end of the formation.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches with the stated alternatives folded into notes of the pitch they replace.

pitch_detail.notes: Up and left on good cracks toward a belay just right of likely cracks through the roof.
Pull the roof at the hand crack, step left into the next crack system and up to a good stance where you can watch the second pull the roof.

Wide crack/slot first (a #5 BD helps); then move left and up the orange face to a crack or thin seam, trending up and right onto much easier terrain, maybe reaching the summit ridge depending on rope drag and length. Loose rock: trundle it.

Scramble north along the ridge and down to a sandy area. From there either traverse the ridge north or walk the sand north until the face pushes you onto slabs on the left; a short downclimb and a gully lead to the ground.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches; the last is a scramble/descent with no grade.
review.other_findings: None; descent is not stored but the text describes the walk-off.

skip_reasons.ca_eagle_peak_4_hanging_rock_5_10_ao: Garbled text; only pitches 1-2 sketched (aid 'AO', then 5.10), third pitch vague; unclear.
